title: CO2 Electroreduction with Enhanced Ethylene and Ethanol Selectivity by Nanostructuring Polycrystalline Copper
abstract: The storage of energy in the form of chemical fuels through the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide could be an attractive alternative to the use of fossil fuels. To achieve high energy density, it is preferable that the fuel be a hydrocarbon, as any oxygen in the fuel reduces its energy density. Extensive research on the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) conducted over the past three decades has shown that only metallic copper can facilitate the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons with high Faradaic efficiencies and reasonable current densities. 4, 5] However, electrochemical reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons on copper requires overpotentials on the order of 1 V and produces a broad product spectrum without high selectivity to any particular product. 4] The published literature also shows that the distribution of products is highly dependent on the manner in which Cu has been pretreated. For example, Kanan and co-workers have shown that oxide-derived Cu nanoparticles are active at overpotentials of ¢0.25 to ¢0.5 V versus RHE for CO2 electroreduction and can produce C2 + oxygenates. [6–8] In similar work, Mul and co-workers have shown that copper nanoparticles deposited on copper plates by electrodeposition of copper oxide films and subsequent electroreduction to copper exhibit an ethylene selectivity of 36 % and an ethylene-to-methane ratio of approximately 30 at an applied potential of ¢1.2 V versus RHE. The major hydrocarbon products produced by the electrochemical reduction of CO2 over Cu are methane and ethylene. Ethylene is an attractive product, because it can be converted to liquid fuels through oligomerization. Methane is not as valuable as ethylene and is readily available from natural gas. Therefore, the design of a catalyst to produce ethylene in high selectivity is an attractive proposition. Recent work has shown that nanostructuring of polycrystalline copper by electrochemical cycling in the presence of Cl¢ anions increases the selectivity to ethylene and suppresses the selectivity to methane. 13] SEM characterization of such nanostructured surfaces shows that they are covered by a large number of cubes exposing Cu(100) facets. This could explain the increased selectivity, because single-crystal studies by Hori and co-workers have shown that Cu(100) surfaces exhibit a high selectivity to ethylene. We note further that in a recent study of the elecThere are a number of recent reports on the use of oxidation/ reduction cycling of Cu surfaces to improve their selectivity for ethylene formation in the aqueous CO2 reduction reaction. Here, the oxidation/reduction process is examined in detail. It is found that the faradaic efficiencies for both ethylene and ethanol are enhanced after oxidation/reduction cycling in the presence of halide anions. Specifically, cycling of the electrode in the presence of chloride, bromide, or fluoride anions allows for an ethylene faradaic efficiency of approximately 15.2 %, a factor of 1.5 higher than that for polycrystalline copper (at ¢1.0 V vs. RHE). The faradaic efficiency for ethanol is also enhanced from 2.65 to approximately 7.6 %. The effects of electrochemical oxidation/reduction with the chloride anion were investigated by using in situ Raman spectroscopy, and the changes in the surface morphology of copper were monitored by using SEM. Consistent with prior reports, it is observed that during the oxidation part of the cycle, anodic corrosion forms a Cu2O layer, which consists of cubical crystals of about 150 nm. During the reduction sweep, it is converted to metallic copper, which forms irregular Cu nanoparticles of around 20 nm in diameter. The enhancement in ethylene formation is presumably attributed to the formation of grain boundaries, which may serve as active sites.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The storage of energy in the form of chemical fuels through the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide could be an attractive alternative to the use of fossil fuels.[1–3] To achieve
high energy density, it is preferable that the fuel be a hydrocarbon, as any oxygen in the fuel reduces its energy density. Ex-
tensive research on the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) conducted over the past three decades has shown
that only metallic copper can facilitate the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons with high Faradaic efficiencies and reasonable current densities.[1, 4, 5] However, electrochemical
reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons on copper requires overpotentials on the order of 1 V and produces a broad product spectrum without high selectivity to any particular product.[1, 4]
The published literature also shows that the distribution of products is highly dependent on the manner in which Cu has
been pretreated. For example, Kanan and co-workers have shown that oxide-derived Cu nanoparticles are active at overpotentials of ¢0.25 to ¢0.5 V versus RHE for CO2 electroreduction and can produce C2 + oxygenates.
[6–8] In similar work, Mul and co-workers have shown that copper nanoparticles deposit-
ed on copper plates by electrodeposition of copper oxide films and subsequent electroreduction to copper exhibit an ethylene selectivity of 36 % and an ethylene-to-methane ratio of approximately 30 at an applied potential of ¢1.2 V versus RHE.[9]
The major hydrocarbon products produced by the electrochemical reduction of CO2 over Cu are methane and ethylene. Ethylene is an attractive product, because it can be converted to liquid fuels through oligomerization.[10] Methane is not as valuable as ethylene and is readily available from natural gas.[11] Therefore, the design of a catalyst to produce ethylene in high selectivity is an attractive proposition. Recent work has
shown that nanostructuring of polycrystalline copper by electrochemical cycling in the presence of Cl¢ anions increases the selectivity to ethylene and suppresses the selectivity to methane.[12, 13] SEM characterization of such nanostructured surfaces shows that they are covered by a large number of cubes ex-
posing Cu(100) facets. This could explain the increased selectivity, because single-crystal studies by Hori and co-workers
have shown that Cu(100) surfaces exhibit a high selectivity to ethylene.[1] We note further that in a recent study of the elec-

The formation of the cubic nanostructures has been attributed to the presence of Cl¢ anions, which results in CuCl formation under oxidizing conditions.[13] The CuCl precipitates as cubes on the surface.[13, 15] The CuCl readily converts to CuOx, which can be reduced to metallic Cu under reducing conditions. The objective of the present work was to examine the
role of halide identity on the nanostructuring of Cu and the consequent effects on both the activity and selectivity of the
restructured Cu for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Our results show that the use of halide anions (F¢ , Cl
¢ , Br¢ , and I¢) to nanostructure polycrystalline copper results in a higher ethylene-to-methane ratio (C2H4/CH4) and an increase in ethanol selectivity.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
For the purpose of this work, we utilize the method outlined
by Roberts et al. to carry out electrochemical cycling of the copper electrode with different halides.[13] Figure 1 shows
cyclic voltammograms (CVs) obtained during the electrochemical cycling of polycrystalline Cu from ¢1.1 to 0.9 V (vs. RHE) in the presence of 4 mm of halide anion. The spikes in the current profiles are attributed to electrolyte convection, owing to the continuous flow of gas through the cell. The CVs show an increase in the oxidative current (F¢> Cl¢> Br¢> I¢) as the anion is changed. Concomitantly, the reduction peak areas in-
crease in the same order according to the anion used and a rough estimate of the thickness of the nanostructured
copper oxide layer can be made by integrating the peak areas
(Table S1). The thickness ranges from 8 to 70 nm. The electrochemically active surface of the copper electrode also increases
as a result of electrochemical cycling, with KCl showing the largest increase and KI the smallest (Table S2).
The product selectivity was determined at ¢1.0 V versus RHE by carrying out constant potential electrolysis for 1.5 h. A potential of ¢1.0 V was chosen because it has been shown previously that this is the potential at which the highest selectivity to ethylene can be achieved.[1, 4] Figures 2 a and 2 d show the current densities and product distributions of electrodes
cycled electrochemically in solutions containing different potassium halides as well as an uncycled electrode (no pretreatment), with specific faradaic efficiency values summarized in
Table S3. It can be seen that electrochemical cycling of the electrode between oxidizing and reducing voltages in KF, KCl,
and KBr results in an increase in current density observed during CO2 reduction. For example, cycling in KCl resulted in a current density of 9.53 mA cm¢2 as compared to that for polycrystalline copper (5.14 mA cm¢2). The geometric current densities of the different electrodes are in the order: KCl >KF
>KBr >KI, no pretreatment. This trend is consistent with the relative surface areas, which were determined by measuring
the double-layer capacitance (Table S2). It is apparent that electrodes cycled electrochemically in KF,
KCl, KBr, and KI exhibit an enhanced faradaic efficiency to ethylene (from 9.4 % to ca. 16.3 %) and ethanol (from 2.65 % to ca. 7.9 %) relative to polycrystalline copper at a potential of ¢1.0 V versus RHE (see Figure 2 d). By contrast, the faradaic efficiency to methane is reduced (from 4.55 % to ca. 0.32 %). The effects
of cycling copper on the distribution of other products can be found in Table S2. We also note that the increases in the fara-
daic efficiencies for ethylene and ethanol are parallel to the increase in thickness of the copper-oxide layer formed during
electrochemical oxidation in the presence of KX (X = F, Cl, Br, I)
(see Tables S1 and S2), a trend previously noted by Yeo and co-workers.[16]
The observation of ethanol as a primary product contrasts with previous studies, which only reported formate anions in the liquid phase.[12, 13, 17] The faradaic efficiency to ethanol increases with the ethylene selectivity, owing possibly to a common intermediate.[18] It was also observed that the fara-
daic efficiency for propanol mirrors that for ethanol, here again suggesting the possibility of a common intermediate with ethanol, which is yet unknown.[4] It is also noted that electrochemical cycling of the electrode resulted in a lower faradaic efficiency for hydrogen evolution.
Figures 2 b and 2 e illustrate the current densities and prod-
uct distributions, respectively, as a function of applied potential for a KF-cycled electrode (specific values in Table S4). As a comparison, the current densities and product distributions for polycrystalline copper are shown in Figures 2 c and 2 f (specific values in Table S5). It is clear from these results that the
overpotential for ethylene formation on the KF-cycled electrode is lower than that found for the unreconstructed Cu elec-
trode. Comparing Figures 2 e and 2 f, it can be seen that the ethylene formation starts at ¢0.8 V for the cycled electrode, whereas ethylene formation is only observed beginning at ¢0.9 V for the control electrode. Comparing the distribution of faradaic efficiencies for polycrystalline copper and copper cycled in KF measured at ¢1.1 V (Figures 2 e and 2 f) indicates that polycrystalline copper exhibits a higher faradaic efficiency

towards carbon-based products than copper cycled in KF. This observation is attributed to the high surface area of the KF-
cycled electrode, which results in a higher current density at an applied voltage of ¢1.1 V. The higher current density leads to severe polarization effects and depletion of CO2 at the surface, owing to increase in the local pH, which in turn reduces the faradaic efficiency for forming carbon-based products.[19]
This effect becomes progressively more important as the applied potential becomes more negative.
Even though the halide-containing electrolyte is removed before CO2 reduction and replaced with a fresh electrolyte (without halide), it is unavoidable that trace amounts of halide
remain. To determine if the presence of halide anions in the electrolyte has an effect on the product selectivity, electrolysis under identical conditions (¢1 V vs. RHE) was carried out with polycrystalline copper in 0.1 m KHCO3 containing 4 mm of KF without prior electrochemical cycling (control). The results for this experiment are shown in Figure 3. For electrodes that

ure 3 b). Next, the maximum oxidizing potential during electro-
chemical cycling was decreased from 0.9 to 0.8 V (vs. RHE) to determine if that had an effect on the product faradaic effi-
ciencies of the KF-cycled electrode. Use of this maximum oxidizing potential did not change the Faradaic efficiencies rela-
tive to that for polycrystalline Cu. At a maximum oxidizing potential of 0.9 V versus RHE, the number of cycles was increased
from 3 to 5 in order to determine if additional cycling would
affect the selectivity. When the number of cycles was increased to 5, the current density increased and the C2H4/CH4 ratio decreased to 12.9. This indicates that there might be an optimal number of cycles for nanostructuring of polycrystalline copper.
Further details concerning the effects of cycling conditions on the product distribution on are shown in Table S6.
It is important to understand how the morphology and
composition of the electrode surface changes during the electrochemical cycling process. It has been proposed previously that CuOx formed during oxidation reduces back to metallic copper under a reducing potential.[13] However, it is unknown
whether Cu2O or CuO forms preferentially or if these oxides remain upon application of a negative potential. In situ Raman
spectroscopy was used to track the changes in the composition of the Cu cathode and the morphological changes were observed by SEM. Raman spectra were acquired as the electrode was cycled from zero applied potential to 1.1 V versus RHE and then down to ¢0.6 V. These experiments were performed in 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte containing 4 mm KCl to enable comparison with similar studies reported earlier.[12, 13]
Linear sweep voltammetry was carried out on the copper
working electrode to various oxidative potentials and then to negative potentials of ¢0.35 and ¢0.6 V. A potential of ¢0.35 and ¢0.6 V allows for partial and full reduction of CuOx on the surface, respectively.[13] At each potential, Raman spectra were
recorded and the morphology of the surface was characterized ex situ by using SEM (Figure 4). At zero applied potential the
Raman spectra of polycrystalline copper showed no obvious features between 100 and 700 cm¢1. However, as the potential was increased past 0.7 V, peaks attributable to Cu2O became visible at 148 cm¢1 (infrared allowed mode), 220 cm¢1 (secondorder Raman-allowed mode), 420 cm¢1 (adsorbed OH¢ species), 521 cm¢1 (second-order overtone mode), and 634 cm¢1 (infrared allowed mode)[20–22] Based on the voltammogram and the Raman spectra, the onset of Cu2O formation is found to begin at around 0.7 V. Increasing the potential from 0.7 to 0.9 V did not lead to the appearance of peaks for CuO, leading to the
conclusion that cycling to 0.9 V produces an oxide layer that
contains predominantly Cu2O. When the potential was increased beyond 0.9 V, formation
of CuO began to occur at 1.0 V (see Figure S2), as confirmed by the appearance of Raman peaks at 290 and 340 cm¢1, corresponding to the zone-centered optical phonon modes of CuO.[23, 24] At the same time, the Raman peak at 148 cm¢1 for Cu2O diminished, which indicates that, with increasing oxidation potential, CuO forms preferentially. We also note that ex situ SEM images taken after oxidation of Cu at 1.0 V show an increased density of CuOx nanocubes and evidence of cubes growing on top of each other (Figure S1). Further in-
creasing the potential to 1.1 V resulted in an even higher density of CuOx nanocubes. The nanocubes now form a very compact layer, although regions with distinct nanocubes can still be clearly observed (Figure S3). At high anodic potentials (1.1 V), evidence for CuO could clearly be seen in the Raman
spectrum through the appearance of peaks at 290 and 340 cm¢1. Reducing the potential from 1.1 or 0.9 V to ¢0.6 V resulted in reduction of the CuxO layer to metallic Cu, as evidenced by the loss of the Raman peaks for CuO and Cu2O. Therefore, it is clear that electrochemical cycling of the elec-
trode results in the formation of metallic copper nanostructures. It is possible that these nanostructures have a large
number of (100) facets, which would explain the high selectivity to ethylene, as suggested by Roberts et al.[1, 13] Another pos-
sibility could be that the nanostructuring process creates a large number of grain boundaries and defects, as proposed

For the ‘control’ case, cycling was not carried out; however, 0.1 m KHCO3 with 4 mm KF was still used as the electrolyte.

by Kanan and co-workers to explain an increased CO2RR activity upon reduction of previously oxidized Cu.[6–8, 25, 26]
The nanostructuring process was also characterized by using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). XPS survey scans and
narrow scans of Cu 2p and Cl 2p were carried out on polycrystalline copper and copper at various stages of the nanostruc-
turing process (Figure S4). Narrow-energy scans of the Cl 2p peaks show that oxidation to 0.9 and 1.1 V results in the appearance of Cl on the surface. This can be attributed to residual CuCl within the CuOx surface layer. Once the surface is fully reduced to metallic Cu at ¢0.6 V, the Cl 2p peak disappears. The Cu 2p peaks of the oxidized electrode are shifted to posi-
tive values of around 0.1 eV compared to polycrystalline copper and fully reduced metallic copper, which is consistent with what has been reported in the literature for Cu2O.
[27] The relatively small shift in binding energies means that Cu 2p peaks for all samples analyzed are very similar. Interestingly, even though formation of CuO was detected in the Raman spectra of copper cycled to 1.1 V, no peaks in the Cu 2p narrow scan could be attributed to CuO,[27] possibly owing to the thinness of this layer.
The effects of halide concentration on the nanostructuring
process were also examined. These experiments were performed by electrochemical cycling in 0.4 and 16 mm KCl (Figure S5). The oxidation current at 0.9 V was found to decrease in the order 16> 4> 0.4 mm, consistent with previous studies of the anodic corrosion of copper in halide-containing media.[28] Upon oxidation to 0.9 V, it is observed by SEM that
a higher electrolyte halide concentration results in a surface
with a higher density of Cu2O. Furthermore, cycling without a halide present does not result in significant anodic corrosion, which is consistent with previous reports[13] . Based on the observations from in situ Raman spectroscopy,
SEM observations of surface morphology changes, and XPS measurements, we envision the following mechanism for the

During electrochemical cycling (Figure 1), it was observed that the oxidation current was highest for F¢ and lowest with I¢ . This pattern can be attributed to differences in the solubilities of the copper halides. When an oxidative potential is applied to copper in the presence of halide anions (X¢), solid CuX forms on the surface of Cu. This CuX layer converts to CuOx and acts as a surface passivation layer, which inhibits further dissolution of the polycrystalline copper below. However, this
passivation layer does not completely cover the surface, because CuX is soluble to a certain extent. The solubilities of the CuX species decrease in the order CuF2> CuCl> CuBr> CuI (see Table S7). For example, evidence for dissolved CuCl has been reported, whereas no evidence for dissolved CuBr and CuI has been reported for similar conditions.[28] For the case of F¢ , CuF2 forms because of the inherent instability of CuF. [31–33] As CuF2 is the most soluble halide salt of Cu, the CuOx films it forms would be expected to be the most porous and, there-
fore, to promote further dissolution of copper (see Scheme 2). This may explain why cycling with F¢ results in a somewhat lower CO2RR current density compared to cycling with Br¢ and Cl¢ , as shown in Figure 2 a, as more of the CuX layer could potentially dissolve away prior to formation of CuOx. We also investigated the morphology of the CuOx layer that forms with different halides (Figure S6). It was observed that, with the exception of F¢ , the CuOx layer takes on a cubic morphology of similar particle size to that found for cycling in Cl¢ . For F¢ , rounded nanoparticles were obtained instead, each nanoparticle seemingly composed of numerous nanograins. The density of the CuOx cubes on the surface follows the order (according to decreasing density) Cl¢> Br¢> I¢ . Therefore, a higher oxidation current would result in a higher density of CuOx cubes. When CuOx was reduced electrochemically, we observed that for all halides, only rounded Cu nanoparticles remained (Fig-
ure S7). The key changes upon nanostructuring are an increase in
current density and an increased selectivity towards C2 products. The increase in current density can be explained simply
by an effective increase in electrochemical surface area. After nanostructuring, the nanoparticles that cover the surface are
expected to have a higher surface area than the previously flat
polycrystalline copper surface. The increased C2 selectivity, on the other hand, could be attributed to the exposure of
a higher number of Cu(100) facets, which have previously been shown to be more selective for such products.[1] Another
factor could be the introduction of a large number of defects and grain boundaries during the nanostructuring process,
which could serve as highly selective active sites for C2 product formation, as suggested by Kanan and co-workers.[26]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text:
We have shown that the restructuring of polycrystalline Cu that occurs upon cycling from oxidizing to reducing potentials
in a potassium halide solution is sensitive to the identity of the halide anion. The degree of restructuring increases in the order I¢ <Br¢ <Cl¢ <F¢ , paralleling the increasing solubility of the corresponding copper halide salt, which results in a corresponding increase in the thickness of the Cu2O layer formed. Evidence from XPS and Raman spectroscopy suggests that the restructuring of Cu begins with halide-induced corrosion and deposition of the copper halide salt once the solubility of the salt is surpassed. The salt crystals then rapidly undergo hydrolysis to form Cu2O and, at higher potentials, CuO. The oxide crystals formed are cubic in shape and when reduced electro-
chemically result in the formation of irregular Cu nanoparticles
(ca. 20 nm in diameter) with rounded edges. Irrespective of the halide anion used during the restructuring of Cu, the Cu nano-
particle formed after restructuring exhibit somewhat higher overall electrochemical activity, a reduction in the faradaic effi-
ciency for H2 formation, and a corresponding increase in the faradaic efficiency for CO2 reduction. Most notably, restructuring leads to a significant suppression in the formation of meth-
ane and a corresponding increase in the formation of ethylene, consistent with much of the recent literature.[12, 13, 17] Cycling of
the electrode in the presence of chloride, bromide, or fluoride anions results in a faradaic efficiency for ethylene of approxi-
mately 15.2 %, a factor of approximately 1.5 higher than that observed for polycrystalline copper (at ¢1.0 V vs. RHE). The faradaic efficiency for ethanol is also enhanced (from 2.65 % to
ca. 7.6 %).

sections.heading: Experimental Section
sections.text:
Potassium carbonate ( 99.995 % metals basis), potassium fluoride dihydrate (98 %), potassium chloride ( 99.0 %), potassium bromide ( 99.0 %), and potassium iodide ( 99.0 %) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Phosphoric acid (85.0–87.0 % assay) was purchased from J.T. Baker. Copper foil (0.1 mm thick, 99.9999 % metals basis) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. Carbon dioxide (99.995 %), nitrogen (99.999 %), helium (99.999 %), and hydrogen (99.999 %) were purchased from Praxair. Hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide gas purifiers were purchased from Valco Instruments Co. Inc. All chemicals were used without further purification. Electrolyte solutions were prepared with 18.2 MW deionized water from a Millipore system. 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte solution was prepared by bubbling 0.05 m K2CO3 solution with CO2 gas for at least 2 h or until a pH of 6.8 was achieved. Electrolyte solution containing 4 mm of halide anion was prepared by adding the appropriate mass of potassium halide salt to 0.1 m KHCO3 solution.
Copper foil (99.9999 %) was cut into electrodes of 2 cm Õ 2 cm squares and cleaned by sonicating for 30 min in acetone, followed by isopropanol, and finally in deionized water. The electrodes were then electropolished in concentrated phosphoric acid at a potential of 2.0 V for 5 min with a copper-foil counter electrode. Next, the electrodes were rinsed with deionized water and dried with a stream of nitrogen. Nanostructuring of electropolished polycrystalline copper was carried out in situ prior to carrying out the electroreduction of CO2 in a 0.1 m KHCO3 solution containing 4 mm
KCl. The electrolyte was first sparged with CO2 until the pH reached 6.8. Prior to carrying out CO2 reduction, each polycrystalline copper electrode was cycled between ¢1.1 and 0.9 V (vs. RHE) at 20 mV s¢1 for three cycles. The electrolyte was then removed and fresh 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte without halide was added for CO2 electroreduction. The morphology of the nanostructured and electropolished polycrystalline copper electrodes was examined by using a FEI Quanta 200 FEG scanning electron microscope.
Electrochemical measurements were carried out by using a Biologic SP-300 potentiostat. Ambient-pressure CO2 electrolysis was carried out in a custom-made, gas-tight electrochemical cell made of polycarbonate and fitted with VitonÒ o-rings. The configuration of the electrochemical cell is such that the working electrode is parallel with respect to the counter electrode (platinum foil) to ensure a uniform potential distribution across the surface. The geometric surface area for both of the electrodes was 1.13 cm2. A Selemion AMV anion-exchange membrane (110 mm thickness) was used to separate the anodic and cathodic compartments. Each of the compartments in this cell contains a small volume of electrolyte (1.3 mL each) to concentrate liquid products and, therefore, increase detection limits. The headspace of the cathodic compartment was approximately 3 mL. Before conducting CO2 electrolysis, the electrolyte in the cathodic compartments was purged with CO2 for at least 15 min. During electrolysis, CO2 was bubbled through the electrolyte at a flow rate of 5 sccm to prevent CO2 depletion. The flow rate of CO2 was controlled with a mass flow controller (Alicat Scientific), and the gas was first humidified with water by passing it through a water-filled bubbler to minimize evaporation of the electrolyte. For all experiments, platinum foil was used as the counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl electrode (leak free series) from Innovative Instruments, Inc. was used as the reference. Data were converted to the RHE reference scale by using the equation: Evs. RHE = Evs. Ag/AgCl + 0.197 V + 0.0591 Õ pH (6.8). To ensure the accuracy of the reference electrodes, calibration was performed with a homemade reversible hydrogen electrode. Prior to any electrolysis, the solution resistance was first determined using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy by scanning from 1 MHz to 10 Hz. For all reported CVs and electrolysis, measurements were made with the potentiostat set to compensate for 85 % of the measured IR drop.
Analysis of gaseous products was carried out with a gas chromatograph (SRI instruments) equipped with a packed HaySep D column and a packed MolSieve 5 A column. A flame ionization detector (FID) with a methanizer was used to detect hydrocarbons (CO, CH4, C2H4, and C2H6) with He as the carrier gas. A thermal conductivity detector (TCD) was used to detect hydrogen with nitrogen as the carrier gas. Calibration of the gas chromatograph was performed by using calibration gas from Praxair (UN 1956) with 0.1 % CO, 0.099 % ethane, 0.099 % ethylene, 0.1 % hydrogen, 0.1 % methane, and balance as helium. Additional calibration points were obtained by dilution of the calibration gas with appropriate flow rates of helium. Further calibration for hydrogen was performed with a calibration mixture obtained from Praxair (UN 1956) containing 500 ppm of hydrogen in nitrogen. After passing through the cell, CO2 flowed directly into the gas sampling loop of the gas chromatograph for online gaseous product analysis, which was carried out every 30 min. For all experiments, electrolysis was allowed to proceed for 1.5 h with gas analysis performed at 10, 35, 60, and 85 min. Data obtained for all durations were averaged to obtain the faradaic efficiencies of the various products. In the timeframe of our experiments, significant differences in the products observed during the course of the run were not observed.

The liquid products were collected from the cathode and anode chambers after electrolysis and analyzed by using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with an UltiMate 3000 instrument from Thermo Scientific. Vials with the collected samples were placed in an autosampler holder and 10 mL of sample was injected into the column. An Aminex HPX 87-H column (Bio-Rad) was used together with diluted sulfuric acid (1 mm) as the eluent. The temperature of the column was maintained at 60 8C in a column oven, and the separated compounds were detected with a refractive index detector (RID). The expected products of CO2RR were also analyzed by using HPLC to produce a standard calibration curve at 60 8C (i.e. formate, acetate, ethylene glycol, ethanol, and n-propanol).
Combined Raman spectroscopy and electrochemical studies were carried out in an epoxy-free Teflon cell.[34] A 5 mm polycrystalline copper disc sheathed in Teflon was used as the working electrode. Before any experiment, the copper disc was first mechanically and subsequently electrochemically polished in concentrated phosphoric acid. All Raman experiments were carried out in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 with 4 mm KCl. In situ Raman spectra of the electrodes were recorded by using a confocal Raman microscope (LabRam HR, Horiba Jobin Yvon). Further details concerning the procedure can be found in Ref. [34].
XPS was performed with a Kratos Axis Ultra DLD utilizing a monochromatized Al Ka source (hn= 1486.6 eV). A takeoff angle of 08 relative to the surface normal was utilized to sample the maximum surface depth.
Surface-area measurements relative to polycrystalline copper were determined by measuring double-layer capacitance values as described by Kanan and co-workers.[7, 8] This was done by using cyclic voltammetry in a potential range where faradaic processes do not occur. The same electrochemical cell as the one used for CO2RR was utilized. However, in this case, a Nafion proton-exchange membrane was used and 0.1 m HClO4 was used as the electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry was carried out at different scan rates and the geometric current density was plotted as a function of scan rate. The slope of this graph is equivalent to the double layer capacitance.
